title: Creation and evolution
hook: many Christians accept evolution as God's way of creating; others read Genesis more literally

segments.voice: Yesterday, out of nothing: the world isn't God and isn't an accident, but a gift. Your line was from nothing, for love. What did you hold and call a gift? Day one thousand seventy-four.

A shell, pressed into stone, sitting on a museum shelf with a little card beside it. A family stops to look. One child reads the card aloud. Another asks, but didn't God make the world in six days? And the parents glance at each other, because they read Genesis differently, and they both go to the same church. A moment like that can happen in any family that shares a pew. It isn't a fight between church and science, at least not in that family. It's a question about how to read a very old page. Today, two words that often get set against each other: creation and evolution.

Genesis opens with days. Light on the first, sky on the second, land and plants on the third, and on through to the seventh, when God rests. Christians who disagree here can both call that chapter true. They differ on what kind of true. Some Christians read the days as ordinary days, and the earth as young, and they see evolution as a story that doesn't fit the page. They take the text at its plainest, and they say that's how they honor it. Other Christians accept evolution as the way God made living things, over a very long time. They read the days as a pattern, a week of work and rest, telling who made the world and why, not a timetable of how. Both kinds of readers can point to scripture. Readers of plain days point to the commandment in Exodus, in the King James: "For in six days the LORD made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that in them is." Readers of a pattern point to a psalm that says to God: "For a thousand years in thy sight are but as yesterday when it is past." The second letter of Peter says: "one day is with the Lord as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day." And there's an old voice in the conversation. Augustine, bishop of Hippo, wrote a book on the literal meaning of Genesis. In it he warned Christians not to talk nonsense about the natural world in front of people who know it well, because it makes scripture look foolish. He was writing about his own day, not ours. But he took both the page and the world seriously. Under all the arguing, the readers share the thing yesterday taught: whether in six days or across ages, the world is a gift, made on purpose. They believe God is the God of every one of those days.
screen: `READ PLAIN, OR READ AS A PATTERN?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at an old rock or fossil. Find a stone, any stone: on a windowsill, in a garden, in a photograph if that's what you've got. Look at it closely for the whole sit. Notice its color, its cracks, any layers or marks. However you read Genesis, this stone was here before you, and it will likely be here after you. Let that size settle in. If you pray, you can say the psalm line slowly: a thousand years in thy sight are but as yesterday. If you don't, just stay with the stone and the length of time it holds. The bell holds the time.
Creation and evolution. Christians read Genesis in more than one way: some as plain days, some as a pattern that leaves room for evolution. Both say God made the world.
Your line: god of all time. Today, when you see something old, a tree, a hill, a brick wall, give it a second look and let it be older than your worries. Day one thousand seventy-four.

howItsDone: Christians differ on Genesis and evolution: some churches and schools teach a young earth and six ordinary days, while others accept evolution and teach Genesis as God's account of who made the world and why.

original.note: Hebrew: day. The word for each of the days in Genesis 1, read by some as ordinary days, by others as a pattern.

what a scholar hears: Augustine's book on Genesis warns against making scripture look foolish on matters people know from the world.

notes: The index hook says 'many Christians accept evolution'; under the claims rule the script says 'some' and 'other Christians' without counts. Keep or restore 'many' only with a source.
Augustine's warning paraphrased from De Genesi ad litteram 1.19.39; confirm the reference and that the summary is fair.

'Christians who disagree here can both call that chapter true. They differ on what kind of true.' is a broad claim; confirm it is acceptable on this path or soften to 'Christians across these views read it as true'.
Both readings are presented without ranking; the young-earth reading is described in its own terms ('that's how they honor it'). Confirm a Keeper from each side would recognize themselves.
No church documents (e.g., Catholic statements on evolution) are cited, to avoid dates and claims not supported by the day's sources.
